extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of the physical sciences conducting quantitative measurements (experimentalists, surveyors, astronomers, physicists, chemists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing, performing, and interpreting accurate quantitative measurements in the physical sciences, covering methods of measurement, instrument roles, conditions for accuracy, sources of error, and the progressive questions to ask about variable phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to treat a phenomenon quantitatively
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a thing may be greater or less, or twice or thrice as great as another, whenever ratio enters even in the rudest manner, there science will have a quantitative character. Events that either happen or do not happen are non-quantitative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume quantitative methods apply only to exactly measurable quantities; whenever degree or ratio can be considered, adopt quantitative treatment. Distinguish simply logical (existence/happening) questions from questions of degree and amount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical precision as scientific goal
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerical precision is the soul of science — as natural objects exist in space and involve molecular movements measurable in velocity and extent, there is no apparent limit to quantitative extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for ever more precise numerical measurement as science advances; use mathematical methods without abandoning logical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of instruments and invention-driven progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction of new instruments (telescopes, pendulums, micrometers, chronometers, dividing engines, balances, torsion balances, galvanometers, calorimeters, etc.) marks epochs and enables detection of much smaller quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing measurements, consider available instruments and how new or improved instruments can multiply sensitivity and open previously inaccessible measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on unassisted senses
rubrics_metrics.description: The eye and other senses give fallacious indications for brightness, size, colour, and position; e.g., eye adjusts iris, irradiation alters perceived star size, colours dull sensibility for same hues, and observers vary with fatigue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use instrumental measurement to correct or replace naked-sense judgments; treat bare sensory data with caution and correct for varying conditions when possible. Examples/anti-patterns: trusting unaided eye for brightness/size, accepting reports of aurora heights or meteor distances without instrumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors often arise from judgment, not raw sense
rubrics_metrics.description: What is actually seen may be true, but interpreting it wrongly yields error; the senses import varying conditions of unknown amount that must be corrected as with a solid instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for perceptual and cognitive biases; implement procedures allowing required corrections and allowances (standardized protocols, calibration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decompose quantitative inquiry into successive questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative questions branch into many: How much is it compared with its cause? Does it change when cause changes? Does it change in same/opposite direction? Is change proportional? If not, what more complex law holds? (Illustrated with solubility and stellar questions.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When investigating a phenomenon, plan a sequence of progressively detailed quantitative questions (existence → dependence on variables → direction of change → law of change → higher-order terms). Use examples given (solubility vs temperature; star motions: move?, direction?, velocity?, variability?, law?).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three general methods of measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) Increase or decrease the quantity in some determinate ratio to bring it within the scope of senses and equate it with the standard unit (multiplication/subdivision). 2) Discover natural conjunctions of events enabling direct comparison of multiples with the unit. 3) Indirect measurement: measure a different quantity connected by known mathematical relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate class of method for the case: scale the quantity (micrometer, thermometer, levers), exploit natural conjunctions (occultations, transits), or use theoretical relations (infer mass from period, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define the measured magnitude with sharp terminations
rubrics_metrics.description: The magnitude must be exactly defined by sharp terminations or precise marks of inconsiderable thickness; vague or graduated boundaries (e.g., penumbra) make exact measurement impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select measurement opportunities or methods that yield precise boundaries (e.g., moment of occultation) and avoid phenomena lacking definite reference points. Where boundaries are gradual, use repeated/standardized observations to reduce ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to multiply/divide quantities without considerable error
rubrics_metrics.description: To measure accurately we must have means of multiplying or dividing a quantity without considerable error so as to equate it with the standard unit or its multiples/submultiples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure repeatability of unit replication, and that joining units yields an aggregate equal to the sum of parts (additivity). Subdivision requires maintaining accuracy across many small parts (e.g., measuring to thousandth of an inch requires error-free addition of thousandths).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish comparison instruments from standard magnitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruments may effect a comparison between two quantities, while the standard magnitude often forms one of the quantities compared; sometimes an instrument combines both (e.g., circle for angular measure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting or designing instruments, determine whether the device provides a standard unit or only a comparative indication, and ensure traceability of intermediate units to ultimate standards. Examples: photometer compares intensities; transit instrument and stars serve as standards for time/clock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express measurement as ratio/equation between magnitude and standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Every measurement makes known the numerical ratio between the magnitude to be measured and a certain other magnitude (fixed unit or intermediate unit); measurement is effected by equating multiples or submultiples and judging equality by the senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan experiments to establish equality (p = (x/y) q) by appropriate physical operations; use the most reliable sense or transduce to a more convenient sense (e.g., time into space on paper).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the measurement mode corresponding to equation form
rubrics_metrics.description: Several modes of expressing the equation p and q correspond to different measurement procedures: subdivide the unit when standard > measured (screw micrometer, divided circle); multiply the unit when the unit is smaller (surveying chain, standard bars); multiply/divide until unit equals object or make device to measure a known fraction (Wheatstone galvanometer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match method to case: use subdivision (micrometer, thermometer tube fineness) when standard exceeds object; use aggregation (bars, chains) when object is larger; use scaling devices or mechanical advantage to render measurements accessible to senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale extreme magnitudes by mechanical or electrical devices
rubrics_metrics.description: When phenomena are too small, weak, rapid or large for direct sensing, apply devices to increase apparent magnitude (lever trains, fine tubes, multiplying screws) or decrease/slow them (inclined plane for falling bodies, Attwood's machine) or measure a known fraction (Wheatstone's method).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design apparatus that scales the phenomenon into the instrument/senseable range, e.g., use inclined planes to slow motion, levers/gears to amplify expansion, draw off known fraction of electric current for measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer opportunities where precise definition and comparison are easy
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose circumstances that simplify precise definition and comparison (e.g., occultations for sudden disappearance, dark spectral lines as precise points for refractive index measurement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time measurements and select natural events that present sharp, reproducible markers to minimize subjective judgment and boundary ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits: not all phenomena are yet measurable
rubrics_metrics.description: Many natural phenomena have hardly been made the subject of measurement at all (intensity of sound, taste and smell phenomena, atom magnitudes, temperature of spark or sun's photosphere); methods may be tedious or measure only special effects rather than total energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge current methodological limits and be cautious of claims of measurability; if a direct measure is unavailable, seek indirect or partial measures and state limitations explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine multiple observations and apply theory of error
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme accuracy is achieved by multiplication of observations and their skilful combination according to the theory of error; repeated independent measurements should accord closely when conditions are satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for repeated measures and statistical combination (averaging, error analysis) to reduce random error and increase precision; ensure independent methods when possible to check systematic effects.
